title: Pieces won on board A deliver the mate on board B
summary: On board A, Black won White's queen with P@d2+ and N@e4+ and sent it to board B, where White, far behind a few moves earlier, dropped it with Q@g4 and went on to mate. Follow the rooks as well: Bxf7+ on board B gave Black on board A a rook that later took on d1 with Rxd1+, and that captured rook, with a pawn from Bxa3+, gave the mate on a5.
event: HypeBeast 1.1.1 against HypeBeast 1.1.0, 500,000 nodes a move

result.text: White on board B mates; the team of A-Black and B-White wins.

moves.note: Black's attack on White's king on board A starts here: the knight takes on f2, and after Kxf2 the other knight checks with Ne4+ and the king goes back to e1. By its own count Black was about three pawns up.

Its first choice was R@f2, dropping the rook it held. It played Ne3 instead because it expected something to arrive from board B: with a pawn or a rook in hand, Ne3 scored far better than R@f2, and a pawn was its likeliest guess. A rook did come, from Nxf1 on board B, and White dropped R@f2 on its next move with a rook still in hand.

lines.note: The engine's answer for Black, after which White still scored itself about three pawns up.
The first choice: the rook at once on f2, then Rxf7 after hxg4.
A search that ignores the other board checks first with R@e2+ before the same rook play on f2; searched the same way it scored a little below Ne3.

moves.note: Its first choice was P@f2+, giving up its pawn for a check and Qh4+. It expected board B to hand White something before its next move, and with a pawn or a rook in White's hand the pawn sacrifice scored much worse; a5 held up best across those cases. White did receive a rook from Nxf1, and Black received a pawn from gxf7+.

lines.note: White's expected answer, R@f2, is the move White played.
The first choice, the pawn check on f2 followed by Qh4+.
A search that ignores the other board plays Qe7 now, which Black played a move later; searched the same way it scored a little below a5.

moves.note: A second rook had just arrived from Nxf1 on board B, and White dropped R@f2, the move it had put off a turn earlier. By its own count White on board A was now about seven pawns up, its best score of the game.

Its first choice was Qxf1, taking the knight. It took the rook on f7 with check instead, expecting a rook back from board A and a bishop for Black, and both came. Yet at its next move it scored itself about ten pawns down. A fresh search after Bxf7+ finds a knight attack ending N@h3+ gxh3 Qxh3, while a search that ignores the other board played Nf5 and stayed about level. The rook it sent to board A later took on d1, and that capture supplied the rook for the final mate.

lines.note: A fresh search after Bxf7+: Black's knight drops end with N@h3+ gxh3 Qxh3, and White is about fifteen pawns behind by that search.
The first choice, Qxf1, taking the knight.
A search that ignores the other board plays Nf5 and stays about level; Bxf7+ searched the same way scored about sixteen pawns lower.

moves.note: Its first choice was fxe3. Instead the bishop took the rook on f2 with check, sending a rook to its partner on board B, who had just given it one with Bxf7+. On board B that rook came down with R@g6 and later took on g7 with check.

Its first choice was N@e4. It thought a knight would very probably be captured on board B and reach White here, and with a knight in White's hand P@d2+ scored much better than N@e4. The knight came, from Nxe7. White took with Kxd2, and after N@e4+ and Ke1, Nxf2 took White's queen, which went straight to the partner on board B.

lines.note: The engine expected Ke2; in the game White took the pawn with Kxd2 and lost the queen to N@e4+ and Nxf2.
The first choice, N@e4 at once: here too the queen goes for a knight, after P@f2+ Qxf2 Nxf2.
What its search preferred with a knight already in White's hand: P@b2.

moves.note: After P@d2+ Kxd2 N@e4+ Ke1, the knight takes White's queen on f2. The queen goes to White on board B, whose forecast had made that capture more likely than not, and is dropped on its next move with Q@g4. Board B had already turned: White there was about twelve pawns down by its own count at Nxe7+ and has been ahead since Nxf5.

Its own search chose Qe6 because of a knight it hoped would arrive from board A: with a knight in hand Qe6 scored much better, without one much worse than Kh7, and it gave the knight about one chance in three. No knight came, and White, who already held the queen won by Nxf2 on board A, dropped it on g4 at once. A search that ignores the other board preferred Kh7.

lines.note: Its own line, expecting Nxg7.
A search that ignores the other board plays Kh7, which it scored about two pawns better than Qe6 searched the same way.
White's plan at its next move: Q@g4 with the queen from board A, then Nxh6+ and Qxe6 to trade queens.

moves.note: The queen had just arrived from board A, where Nxf2 took White's queen; White's forecast had made that capture more likely than not. On g4 it stands behind the knight on f5, facing Black's queen on e6. Most of the engine's score here was what the captures in its line would give the partner on board A.

lines.note: After B@g6 and Nxh6+, the queens come off on e6 and Qxa1 takes the bishop.
A search that ignores the other board takes on g7 and keeps the queen in hand; searched the same way it scored about a pawn better than Q@g4.

moves.note: By the engine's count the board itself was about level, but almost all of its score, about thirty pawns against it, was what its losses would give board A: a queen or a knight reaching Black there was enough, it counted, to mate its partner. Its line still loses the queen on e6 to Nxh6+ and Qxe6. B@g5 at least lets the bishop take back on h6.

lines.note: Its own line: the queens come off on e6 and White's queen takes on f1.
A search that ignores the other board drops P@g6 instead, with the same trade on e6 to follow; searched the same way it scored slightly below B@g5.

moves.note: This rook came from board B, sent by Bxf7+, and was dropped with R@c1. Taking White's rook on d1 sends that rook to White on board B, who keeps it for the mate R@a5#. After Kxd1, the pawn on b2 promotes with b1=Q+.

The queen on b1 was a promoted pawn, so when White took it with Kxc1, Black on board B received only a pawn. The bishop it captured went to its partner on board B, and by the engine's count one more bishop there was enough to mate. Most of its score came from what such captures were worth to the partner.

lines.note: Its line: after Kxc1, Bxa3+ and pawn drops chase the king to a1.
A search that ignores the other board plays Qf6 and scores nearly the same; it knows nothing of what the bishop is worth on board B.
White's own line at its next move, with the pawn from b7 already in Black's hand: by White's own count Black was still far ahead.

moves.note: Mate in three by the engine's count. Rxb7+ takes a pawn with check, a pawn worth almost nothing on board A by its count, and drives the king to a5. Its line used B@b4+ with the bishop just won on c1; it also expected a pawn to reach it from board A, and one did.

lines.note: The planned mate: Ka5, B@b4+ Ka4, R@a5+.
With a pawn in hand as well, the same mate runs with P@b4+, as in the game.

moves.note: The pawn came from Bxa3+ on board A, as the forecast at its previous move had expected. Dropping it instead of the bishop keeps the bishop in hand, and after Ka4 the rook drop on a5 mates.

The rook came from board A, where Rxd1+ captured White's rook; the black rook that took it had come from Bxf7+ on this board. On board A, Black sat instead of moving: its partner had mate on the next move, and while Black sat, White there could capture nothing to send to the side being mated.
